title: Recursion: Functions That Call Themselves
lead: Recursion is when a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of that problem. Every recursive solution has two parts: a base case that stops the calls, and a recursive case that breaks the problem down.

sections.heading: The core idea
sections.body: Think of Russian nesting dolls: open one and there's a smaller one inside, until you reach the tiniest doll that doesn't open. The base case is that tiny doll — without it, calls go on forever and you get a stack overflow. The recursive case is every doll that opens into another.

sections.heading: How the call stack works
sections.body: Each recursive call is pushed onto the call stack and waits until the call below it returns. For factorial(4), the stack builds up: factorial(4) → factorial(3) → factorial(2) → factorial(1). Then results bubble back up: 1 → 2 → 6 → 24. Deep recursion on large inputs can exhaust the stack — that's when an iterative approach or tail-call optimisation is preferred.

tryThis: Write a recursive function to compute factorial(n). Trace factorial(5) by hand, drawing each call frame on paper. Then identify what happens if you forget the base case.
